title: The milk Vitthal drank
hookLine: a boy sets a bowl of milk before the god, and waits for him to drink
carry: naivedya: God receives what love offers

lines: A BOWL OF MILK FOR VITTHAL.
HE WAITS FOR THE GOD TO DRINK.
cards: A bowl of milk sits on the temple floor at Pandharpur, before the image of Vitthal, the dark god who stands on a brick with his hands on his hips. A small boy has carried it there.
His father usually brings the offering, but he's away, so today the boy has been sent. He sets it down, folds his hands, and waits. The god doesn't move.
The milk doesn't move. The boy keeps waiting. Nobody has told him that offerings are usually received unseen.

teach.h: A FAMILY OF TAILORS, DEVOTED TO VITTHAL.
teach.b: Tradition says Namdev grew up in a family of tailors devoted to Vitthal, the form of Krishna worshiped at Pandharpur, whom devotees call Vithoba, and sometimes mother.
As the story goes, the boy waits, and still the god doesn't drink. So he pleads.
Why won't you take it? Some tellings say he cries; some say he threatens to break his own head on the stone floor if Vitthal refuses.
And Vitthal, the story says, reaches out of the image and drinks the milk. All of it. The boy goes home with an empty bowl, and nobody believes him.
It's funny, and it's also about something Hindus do every day.
It's called naivedya: food is offered to God first, at the home shrine or in the temple, before anyone eats.
Devotees trust that God receives it all the same, and what comes back is prasad, food made holy by being offered, shared with everyone. Namdev's story is the one where a child got to see it received.
He takes Vitthal at his word, the way a child takes anyone at their word, and the story rewards him instead of correcting him. Namdev grows up to be a singer.
His songs, called abhangs, talk to Vitthal like someone in the same room: pleading, teasing, longing. Varkaris still sing them in kirtan, call and response, with cymbals keeping the beat.

how: Varkari devotees sing abhangs, including Namdev's, in kirtan with cymbals, and the temple of Vitthal at Pandharpur keeps a step at its entrance named for Namdev.

games.q: you're the boy Namdev. you've set the milk before Vitthal, and the god hasn't touched it. what do you do?
o: leave it there; that's how offerings work.
keep waiting and pleading until he drinks.
drink it yourself so it isn't wasted.
games.why: he pleads, and the story says Vitthal reaches out and drinks it all. that's naivedya: offered first, and received.

practice: Rest your hands on your knees, palms up, as if holding a small bowl, and think of something simple you'll eat or drink today.

Before you do, you'll hold it up for a moment and offer it, the way the boy did, as if it will really be received; then eat it as prasad. If you pray, offer it to God, by Vitthal's name or any name you already use.
If you don't, offer thanks to whoever grew it or made it.

wordCard.voice: Namdev. The tailor's son of the Marathi saint tradition, who, the story says, waited until Vitthal drank the milk, and grew up singing abhangs.
